subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: Abortion cases encompass spontaneous and induced pregnancy loss. Clinicians must assess timing, cause, and complications, then provide appropriate medical or surgical care and follow‑up. Early recognition prevents morbidity and mortality.

sections.p: Abortion is the loss of a pregnancy before viability, usually before 20 weeks. Diagnosis relies on history, ultrasound, and hCG trends.
Staging follows the WHO classification: I (early), II (mid), III (late). Severity is gauged by haemorrhage, infection, and fetal viability.
b: Stage III: >20 weeks, heavy bleeding or infection

sections.p: Common causes vary by setting. In low‑resource areas, infections and herbal remedies are frequent.
b: Infections: Chlamydia, Gonorrhoea, Syphilis, HIV, TB

sections.p: Symptoms include vaginal bleeding, cramping, and loss of fetal parts. Fever and foul discharge suggest infection.
Tests confirm pregnancy status, haemorrhage, and infection. Availability may be limited; clinical judgment is key.

t.b: Empty uterus = miscarriage; intrauterine gestation = viable
Low Hb = anaemia; high WBC = infection

sections.p: Urgent care is needed if haemorrhage, sepsis, or retained products threaten life.
Treat the underlying cause, control bleeding, and prevent infection. Choice of therapy depends on gestational age and resources.
b: Antibiotics for septic abortion (e.g., penicillin + gentamicin)
Tranexamic acid for haemorrhage control (if available)

t.b: Preferable to blood transfusion when resources limited

sections.p: Post‑abortion care includes contraception counselling, STI screening, and mental health support.
Conditions that mimic abortion include ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy, and retained placenta.
b: Ectopic pregnancy: abdominal pain, amenorrhoea, positive hCG
Molar pregnancy: high hCG, vaginal bleeding, uterine size > dates

sections.p: Low hCG in early pregnancy can be normal; false‑negative STI tests occur with early infection.
b: Early pregnancy hCG may be low but viable
Rapid tests may miss early syphilis or HIV

faq.q: Can an abortion be safe in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Yes, with early medical or manual vacuum aspiration and basic infection control.

faq.q: What if the patient has a fever after abortion?
faq.a: Treat as septic abortion; start broad‑spectrum antibiotics and monitor haemodynamics.

faq.q: Is contraception needed after an abortion?
faq.a: Yes, to prevent unintended repeat pregnancy and reduce future complications.

exam: Explain the WHO staging of abortion and its clinical implications.
Describe the management steps for a patient presenting with a late miscarriage and haemorrhage in a district hospital.
Discuss the differential diagnosis for a woman with vaginal bleeding and cramping after 10 weeks of pregnancy.
